title: How to plan a cross-stitch project
subtitle: Choosing a chart, calculating fabric size, and preparing supplies
excerpt: A cross-stitch project starts before the first stitch: choosing a chart that suits the available time and skill level, calculating how much fabric the design needs, and gathering the floss colours before sitting down at the hoop. Good planning prevents mid-project fabric shortages and the slow frustration of realising a chart was too large for the frame to hand.
sourceNotes: Standard cross-stitch project planning practice. Fabric calculation formula follows the convention established in major needlework suppliers' printed guides.

content.text: Planning a cross-stitch project means three things: choosing a chart you can finish at the skill level and time you have, calculating the right fabric size, and gathering all the
floss
colours before starting. Stopping mid-project to source a discontinued dye lot is the most common cause of half-finished pieces.
Choosing a chart
Chart complexity is measured in three ways: the number of colour changes per row, the presence of
fractional stitches

(quarter and three-quarter crosses), and the total stitch count. For a beginner project, look for a chart with no more than ten colours, no fractional stitches, and a total size under 100 by 100 stitches.
Calculating fabric size
To work out how large the fabric needs to be, divide the chart's stitch count in each direction by the
Aida
count, then add at least 10 cm (4 inches) on all four sides. The extra margin is what goes in the hoop or frame and what will be needed if the piece is to be stretched for framing.

attrs.title: Fabric size formula
attrs.body: Stitch width ÷ fabric count = design width in inches. Add 4 inches on each side for the border. Repeat for height. Example: a chart 100 stitches wide on 14-count Aida: 100 ÷ 14 = 7.1 inches. Add 4 inches each side: 7.1 + 8 = 15.1 inches. Buy at least 16 inches wide.

content.text: Gathering the floss
Read the chart's colour key. Note every DMC (or Anchor) code listed.
Check what you already have in your floss storage. Mark anything missing.

Buy one skein of each missing colour, plus a second skein of any colour the chart indicates in a large filled area (a sky, a background block). Running out of a background colour mid-piece and finding the dye lot has changed is the frustration most experienced stitchers have learned to pre-empt.
Wind each colour onto a floss bobbin or stranding stick and label it with the colour code.

items.symptom: The designed area is larger than the fabric when stitching begins
items.cause: The fabric size was calculated without the border margin.
items.fix: Pause. Calculate the true finished size including the margin and check there is still enough fabric on all sides. If the design has grown beyond the fabric edge, the piece needs to be restarted on larger fabric.

content.text: What to try next
Once the fabric and floss are ready, the next step is
finding the centre of the fabric
and setting up the hoop. For pieces over 100 by 100 stitches, grid the fabric first.

glossaryTerms.definition: The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch. Each skein is made of six strands twisted together loosely; the stitcher strips out the number of strands needed for the fabric count (two strands for 14-count Aida) and threads them together.

A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads. The default for beginners. Counted in squares per inch: 11ct, 14ct, 16ct, and 18ct are the common counts.
